note: License policy for the third-party components compiled into ./cmd/lit — Go modules AND the statically-linked native C libraries (ICU, zstd, musl, compiler-rt; see native.go). Every entry in allowed_licenses is a permissive license with no copyleft obligation that conflicts with lit's MIT 'free for any purpose' guarantee, and every entry is earned: links-licensing-c0ce.9 deleted MPL-2.0, WTFPL, and ISC once measurement showed nothing lit links classified as any of them, because an allowlist naming a license no component carries is a standing invitation to acquire one. Re-measure by generating LICENSE-REPORT.md and reading its summary table — the distinct licenses there are exactly the entries this list should hold. That is a measurement a human runs, deliberately not a gate: `go list -deps` resolves a platform-dependent module set, so a check that every entry is carried by something linked would fail on whichever platform did not need the dependency that earned it. MODULE_EXCEPTIONS IS EMPTY AND STAYS EMPTY. A component whose license (per tools/licenses' classifier for Go modules, or the curated license in native.go for native libs) is not in allowed_licenses fails the gate — `go run ./tools/licenses -check` in release-validate, and TestDependencyLicensesArePermitted on every PR — and the correct response to that red gate is to REMOVE the dependency, not to document it. The failure this file guards against is not a dependency bump. It is a future agent, mid-task, with a red gate and a deadline, thinking 'this module is clearly fine, I'll add an exception with a good reason — that is literally what module_exceptions is for.' It is a reasonable thought and it is how a zero-copyleft tree gets undone one honest-looking entry at a time, because each exception arrives with a persuasive paragraph attached and none of them is individually wrong. Re-opening the array is the owner's call, not an implementer's; TestLoadPolicyEmbedded pins it empty so that re-opening it can only happen as a deliberate, reviewable change. An unclassifiable license — the classifier's 'Unknown' sentinel — is a hard failure with no route around it at all: not an allowlist entry, not an exception. It is the one row an auditor cannot evaluate, so parsePolicy refuses a policy naming it either way — including one hiding as an arm of an expression — and both rulings, Allows and Permits, refuse it again regardless of what any policy says. Nor is 'is this permissive?' left to the reader any more: parsePolicy refuses an allowlist entry the license classifier types as restricted, reciprocal or FORBIDDEN, which is every GPL, LGPL, MPL, EPL and AGPL. That check is a VETO and not the authority, because the taxonomy is a corporate policy rather than a copyleft test — it has no opinion at all about Unicode-3.0 or about any compound expression, and it calls WTFPL forbidden though WTFPL is permissive — so it refuses only what nobody here would defend and never fires on a license it simply does not know. Matching is by EXACT STRING, never by parsing SPDX: an entry may be a single identifier or a whole expression (compiler-rt's 'MIT AND Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception' is the only expression today), so a semantically identical rewording — reordered arms, a different spacing — is a different string and fails the gate with a misleading non-allowlisted-license message. Copy an expression exactly as native.go states it. Because nothing downstream ever parses an entry, an expression would otherwise allowlist a COMBINATION without the gate vetting its arms, so parsePolicy enforces two rules on one: every AND-arm's base identifier must be independently present in this list (a WITH-exception only widens a grant, so 'Apache-2.0' satisfies the arm 'Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception'), and an OR is refused outright — lit resolves a dual license to the elected arm before it reaches policy, recording a single identifier plus acknowledgement 'concluded' (see zstd in native.go), so an OR entry means an election went unmade. Know one consequence before following the re-measure procedure above: an AND-arm's base is required by the parse whether or not anything carries that identifier BARE, so a base present only to satisfy an expression is earned by that expression and is not an unused entry — deleting it as unmeasured makes the file fail to load, which breaks -check and -graph together rather than merely reopening the gate. Read that requirement the other way too. A future compound of the form 'MIT AND <something>' forces a bare '<something>' entry into this list, and a bare entry permits that license on ANY linked module, so adding such an expression widens the gate further than the one component it was added for. If that is ever unwelcome, the expression is the thing to reconsider, not the base. Expression entries are also inert in the module-graph audit, whose per-file classifications are always single identifiers. This is the single committed policy file; edit it to accept a new license class that something lit ships now carries. See links-supply-chain-w6m9.3 and w6m9.4.
